body:
Why farmers depended on credit

Many colonial-era cultivators needed money before harvesting their crops. They borrowed to obtain seeds and other inputs, pay land revenue or rent, meet household expenses and survive periods of poor income.

Credit was commonly supplied by moneylenders, merchants and commercial agents. Borrowing could help a cultivator continue production, but it could also create dependence if the interest burden was high or repayment was demanded when crop prices were low.

How commercialisation increased market dependence

A farmer producing mainly for household consumption retained at least part of the harvest as food. A farmer producing a commercial crop depended more directly on the price offered by buyers. This difference became important when export demand changed unexpectedly.

If cotton prices rose, a farmer who produced cotton might obtain greater income. But if the farmer had borrowed heavily and cotton prices later declined, the proceeds from the crop might be insufficient to repay the debt. Therefore, high commercial demand in one year did not guarantee lasting prosperity.

Example: Cotton during the American Civil War

The American Civil War began in 1861 and disrupted the supply of American raw cotton to British textile factories. British manufacturers sought additional cotton from India.

Indian cotton exports increased and prices rose. Merchants and moneylenders extended advances to cultivators in cotton-growing areas, including the Deccan, encouraging greater production for the market.

After the war ended in 1865, American cotton supplies recovered. The exceptional demand for Indian cotton weakened, prices declined and credit became harder to obtain. Some lenders demanded repayment of outstanding debts.

This sequence illustrates a central risk of commercial agriculture: a cultivator may expand production and borrowing during a price boom, only to face financial difficulty when demand and prices change.

Why commercial farming could increase food vulnerability

Food vulnerability means an increased risk that households will be unable to obtain sufficient food. Commercialisation could contribute to such vulnerability under certain conditions.

  • Competition for land: Expansion of commercial crops could reduce the land available for food crops in some localities.
  • Income instability: Falling crop prices could leave households with insufficient money to purchase food.
  • Debt obligations: Loan repayment, rent and revenue demands could force cultivators to sell produce even when their own consumption needs were not fully met.
  • Unequal market power: Merchants and lenders could obtain more favourable terms than indebted small cultivators.
  • Poor agricultural conditions: Low productivity, weak irrigation and crop failure could further reduce food availability and household income.

Commercialisation did not automatically cause famine

Growing crops for sale does not necessarily reduce food security. Commercial farming can increase income when farmers receive adequate prices and retain access to food. Vulnerability becomes greater when commercial pressure combines with inadequate food production, unstable earnings, debt, poor access to markets or reduced purchasing power.

Why rural outcomes were unequal

Large landholders, traders and prosperous cultivators could sometimes gain from rising prices and expanding trade. Small cultivators, tenants and agricultural labourers were more exposed to high rent, limited savings and unstable employment.

Some former artisans also moved into agriculture after losing craft occupations. This increased pressure on rural employment and land, particularly where alternative industrial jobs were scarce.

Prelims focus

  • The American Civil War lasted from 1861 to 1865.
  • Disruption of American cotton supplies increased British demand for Indian raw cotton.
  • Indian cotton prices rose during the wartime supply disruption.
  • After American supplies recovered, Indian cotton demand weakened and rural credit became more restricted.
  • Debt and unstable prices could increase the vulnerability of small cultivators.
  • Trap: A rise in cash-crop production does not necessarily mean that every farmer's income or food security improved.

[Sources: NCERT, Craft Traditions of India: Past, Present and Future, Class 11, Ch. 2, Colonial Rule and Crafts, sections The Impact of Colonialism on the Textile Trade and Credit Dries Up, pp. 23–25; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, Ch. The Age of Industrialisation, section 3.3, pp. 116–117; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Ch. 1, section 1.3, Agricultural Sector, pp. 5–7; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Ch. 3, Ruling the Countryside, pp. 27–30 and 33–35.]

pictures.alt: In 1861, war boosted Indian cotton demand, prices and advances; after 1865, recovering American supplies brought falling prices and repayment demands.
pictures.caption: The American Civil War shows how distant events affected Indian cotton farmers and rural credit.

title: Rural Credit, Cotton Prices and Food Vulnerability

body:
The economy India inherited in 1947

When India became independent on 15 August 1947, its economy remained predominantly agricultural. Traditional handicrafts had experienced serious decline, modern industry was inadequately developed, and a large share of the population depended on low-productivity rural occupations.

The economy also reflected decades of colonial trade and financial policies. Agriculture and commerce were linked to overseas markets, while industrial production, education, public health and infrastructure required substantial improvement.

Low growth and heavy dependence on agriculture

Estimates discussed in NCERT indicate that during the first half of the 20th century, India's aggregate real output generally grew at less than 2% annually, while growth in per capita output was approximately 0.5% annually. These are broad historical estimates, not figures for a single year.

Around 85% of the population lived mainly in villages and depended directly or indirectly on agriculture for their livelihood. However, the share of the workforce in agriculture was generally estimated at 70–75% during the colonial period.

SectorApproximate share of colonial workforceMain condition
Agriculture70–75%Dominant occupation; low productivity
Manufacturing10%Weak industrial base; decline of many handicrafts
Services15–20%Relatively limited occupational share

These are approximate historical ranges, not exact figures from a single census year. The percentages should not be mechanically added together using the highest value in each range.

85% and 70–75% describe different things. The first concerns the population living mainly in villages and deriving a livelihood from agriculture; the second concerns the proportion of working people employed in agriculture.

Condition of agriculture

Agricultural productivity was low. Much of the sector depended on traditional methods, while irrigation, investment and modern inputs were inadequate in many regions. Cultivators often faced rent, revenue and debt obligations.

Commercialisation had increased links with markets, but its benefits were uneven. Expansion in the area under cultivation did not always mean a corresponding improvement in productivity or household welfare.

Condition of industry

Modern industries such as cotton textiles, jute and iron and steel had appeared, but their overall development remained limited. The decline of traditional handicrafts had not been matched by sufficient expansion in modern manufacturing employment.

Capital-goods industries, which produce machinery and equipment used to make other goods, were especially underdeveloped. India therefore lacked a broad industrial base capable of supporting rapid expansion across many sectors.

Foreign trade and infrastructure

India's foreign trade was substantially oriented towards supplying raw materials and purchasing manufactured products. Colonial financial obligations also involved outward transfers of income.

Railways, ports, roads and communication networks had expanded, but much of their development served strategic, administrative and commercial needs of the colonial government. These facilities also created useful transport and communication links, although they remained inadequate for the needs of the entire population.

Social conditions

Education and health indicators were poor. Historical estimates presented in NCERT indicate an overall literacy level of less than 16%, female literacy of approximately 7% and life expectancy of approximately 32 years during the late colonial period. These figures describe broad conditions of the time and should not be treated as exact results of a census conducted on Independence Day.

Poverty, unemployment, inadequate public health facilities and vulnerability to food shortages were major challenges facing the newly independent country.

An immediate economic effect of Partition

Partition in 1947 disrupted important agricultural and industrial linkages. Much of the jute-growing area of undivided Bengal became part of East Pakistan, now Bangladesh, while important jute mills remained in India. This created a shortage of nearby raw jute for mills on the Indian side.

This illustrates the economic difference between the location of raw-material production and the location of manufacturing industries. A change in political boundaries could separate the two and disrupt production.

Understanding the overall relationship

The drain of wealth, deindustrialisation and commercialisation of agriculture were connected aspects of colonial economic change. Outward financial transfers limited resources available for domestic use. Competition from British manufactured goods weakened many traditional industries. Commercial agriculture connected rural producers to distant markets but also exposed them to price changes and credit dependence.

By 1947, India had some modern factories and transport facilities, but it remained an overwhelmingly agrarian economy with substantial industrial, agricultural and social-development needs.

Prelims focus

  • India became independent on 15 August 1947.
  • Agriculture accounted for approximately 70–75% of the colonial workforce; manufacturing accounted for about 10%.
  • Approximately 85% of the population lived mainly in villages and depended directly or indirectly on agriculture.
  • During the first half of the 20th century, annual growth of real output was estimated at less than 2%, with per capita growth of about 0.5%.
  • Partition separated much of the jute-growing area in East Pakistan from major jute mills in India.
  • Trap: The existence of railways and some modern factories did not mean that India possessed a well-developed industrial economy at Independence.

[Sources: NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Ch. 1, Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence, sections 1.2–1.9, pp. 5–13; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Ch. 6, Weavers, Iron Smelters and Factory Owners, pp. 72–79; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, Ch. The Age of Industrialisation, sections 4–5.1, pp. 118–123.]

pictures.alt: Three colonial pathways—wealth drain, deindustrialisation and commercialisation—converge on India's agricultural economy and weak industry in 1947.
pictures.caption: The colonial economic pattern helps explain the challenges India faced in 1947.

title: The Indian Economy at Independence: Main Conditions and Colonial Legacies
